title.zh: 卷二十二 志第十二 樂上
title.raw: 卷二十二 志第十二 樂上 Volume 22 Treatises 12: Music Part One

translations.literal: Music Treatise, Part One
translations.idiomatic: Treatise on Music: Part One

sentences.zh: 夫性靈之表，不知所以發於詠歌；

translations.literal: As for the outward manifestation of innate spiritual nature, one does not know by what means it finds expression in songs of praise;
translations.idiomatic: The outward stirrings of our inner nature break into song before we can say why.

sentences.zh: 感動之端，不知所以關於手足。

translations.literal: as for the beginnings of being stirred and moved, one does not know by what means they connect with hands and feet.
translations.idiomatic: The first thrill of being moved seizes the limbs before we can trace how it got there.

sentences.zh: 生於心者謂之道，成於形者謂之用。

translations.literal: What is born in the heart is called the Way; what takes finished form in the body is called its function.
translations.idiomatic: What arises within the mind they call the Way; what takes shape in outward bearing they call its functioning.

sentences.zh: 譬諸天地，其猶影響，百獸率舞，而況於人乎！

translations.literal: Compare it to Heaven and Earth—it is like shadow and echo; the hundred beasts all dance in time—how much more so mankind!
translations.idiomatic: Think of Heaven and Earth: music follows stimulus as surely as shadow or echo; even beasts fall into step and sway—need anyone speak of human beings?

sentences.zh: 美其和平而哀其喪亂，以茲援律，乃播其聲焉。

translations.literal: They praise its harmony and peace and lament its loss in turmoil; taking this as support for pitch pipes, they thereby spread abroad its sounds.
translations.idiomatic: People cherish peace and harmony and mourn the ruin music suffers in chaos; on that basis they align the tubes of pitch and send those sounds abroad.

sentences.zh: 農瑟羲琴，倕鐘和磬，達靈成性，象物昭功，由此言之，其來自遠。

translations.literal: The farmers’ se, Fuxi’s qin, Chui’s bells and harmonizing chimes—penetrating to spiritual intelligence and completing nature, imaging creatures and displaying merit—from this it may be said that they come from afar.
translations.idiomatic: From the se of the husbandmen and Fuxi’s zither to Chui’s bells and tuned sonorous stones, music reaches through spirit to complete human nature, figures things in sound and proclaims their merit—so its origins lie deep in antiquity.

sentences.zh: 殷氏不綱，遺風餘孽，淫奏既興，雅章奔散，《英》《莖》之制，蓋已微矣。

translations.literal: The Yin house lost its guiding cord; surviving customs and lingering abuses flourished; wanton performances arose and canonical pieces scattered—the compositions “Ying” and “Jing” had already grown faint.
translations.idiomatic: When the Yin lost proper governance, decadent strains lingered; licentious performance drove out stately ritual music, and classics such as “Ying” and “Jing” faded almost beyond recall.

sentences.zh: 孔子曰：「人能弘道，非道弘人。

translations.literal: Confucius said: “It is the person who can enlarge the Way—not the Way that enlarges the person.”
translations.idiomatic: Confucius said, “Human beings broadened the Way; it was never the Way that broadened human beings.”

translations.literal: ” From the Zhou, the two parts of the “Nan” began; the “Airs” embraced six ages.
translations.idiomatic: With the Zhou came the paired “Nan” sections of the Book of Songs, and the “Airs” gathered poetry spanning six eras.

sentences.zh: 昔黃帝作《雲門》，堯作《咸池》，舜作《大韶》，禹作《大夏》，殷作《大濩》，周作《大武》，所謂因前王之禮，設俯仰之容，和順積中，英華髮外。

translations.literal: In antiquity the Yellow Emperor made “Cloud Gate”; Yao made “Mulberry Pool”; Shun made “Grand Shao”; Yu made “Grand Xia”; Yin made “Grand Hu”; Zhou made “Grand Wu”—what is called inheriting the former kings’ ritual, setting out gestures of bowing and rising, storing harmony and compliance within, and letting splendid brilliance burst forth without.
translations.idiomatic: Legend credits the Yellow Emperor with “Cloud Gate,” Yao with “Mulberry Pool,” Shun with “Grand Shao,” Yu with “Grand Xia,” Yin with “Grand Hu,” and Zhou with “Grand Wu”—music that continued older court ritual, choreographed every inclination of the body, hoarded gentle obedience inwardly, and let splendor shine outward.

sentences.zh: 《書》稱命夔典樂，教胄子，則《周官》所謂奏大呂，歌黃鐘。

translations.literal: The Documents records the command to Kui to preside over music and instruct the noble heirs—thus what the Offices of Zhou calls presenting great lu and singing huangzhong.
translations.idiomatic: The Book of Documents tells how Kui was ordered to direct ritual music and train the heirs apparent—the same tradition the Rites of Zhou names when it speaks of sounding dalu and singing huangzhong.

sentences.zh: 天貺來下，人祗動色，抑揚周監，以弘雅音。

translations.literal: Heaven’s gift descended; spirits and men alike were stirred; raising and lowering followed Zhou models to amplify refined tones.
translations.idiomatic: Heaven sent down its blessing; gods and men showed awe on their faces; lifting and lowering the pitch followed Zhou precedent to magnify the classical sound.

sentences.zh: 及褒豔興災，平王逢亂，禮廢親疏，樂沈河海。

translations.literal: When favor to Bao Si brought calamity and King Ping met disorder, ritual collapsed between kin close and distant, and music sank into rivers and seas.
translations.idiomatic: When favor lavished on Bao Si invited disaster and King Ping’s reign dissolved in turmoil, ritual collapsed between close kin and remote branches, and instruments of music were drowned as if in flood tide.

sentences.zh: 是以延陵季子聞歌《小雅》曰：「其周德之衰乎！

translations.literal: Therefore when Jizi of Yanling heard the song “Lesser Odes,” he said: “Is this not the decline of Zhou virtue!
translations.idiomatic: So when Prince Jizi of Yanling heard the “Lesser Elegantiae,” he declared, “This is Zhou virtue in decay.

translations.literal: Yet traces of the former kings’ lingering influence remain.”
translations.idiomatic: Yet something of the old kings’ influence still lingers in it.”

translations.literal: ” Then each feudal domain styled itself a lone heir and raised its own songs and chants.
translations.idiomatic: Afterward each lord who carved out a realm sang his own verses and raised his own hymns.

sentences.zh: 魏文侯聆古樂而恐臥，晉平公聽新聲而忘食，先王之道，漸以陵夷。

translations.literal: Marquis Wen of Wei listened to ancient music and grew drowsy; Duke Ping of Jin heard novel strains and forgot to eat—the Way of the former kings slipped away by degrees.
translations.idiomatic: Marquis Wen of Wei grew sleepy listening to classical pieces; Duke Ping of Jin skipped meals for fashionable novelty—the teaching of the ancient kings ebbed away step by step.

translations.literal: The eight directions differ in prevailing winds; the nine provinces diverge in local norms.
translations.idiomatic: Every quarter of the realm had its wind; every province its distinct usage.

sentences.zh: 秦氏併吞，遂專刑憲，至於弦歌《詩》《頌》，幹戚旄羽，投諸煙火，掃地無遺。

translations.literal: When Qin swallowed all rivals, it monopolized punishments and statutes; as for strumming the Odes and Hymns or wielding shields, plumes, and yak-tail banners, they were pitched into smoke and flame until nothing remained.
translations.idiomatic: Once Qin conquered every rival, it seized sole control of law and penalty; songs from the Classic of Poetry, dances with shields and spears, and feathered regalia were heaped on bonfires until the tradition was swept bare.

sentences.zh: 漢祖提劍寰中，削平天下，文匪躬於德化，武有心於製作。

translations.literal: The Han founder seized the sword within the realm and leveled the empire; in civil affairs he did not personally labor at moral transformation, yet in military matters he still harbored designs for institutional creation.
translations.idiomatic: Liu Bang raised arms inside the empire and crushed rival kings; though he never bent personally to gentle moral instruction, his martial mind still toyed with founding new institutions.

sentences.zh: 太后擯儒家之道，大臣排賈氏之言，搢紳先生所以長歎，而子政、仲舒猶不能已也。

translations.literal: The empress dowager cast aside Confucian teaching; great ministers rejected Jia Yi’s proposals—hence the long sighs of cap-and-girdle scholars, while Zizheng and Zhongshu still could not contain themselves.
translations.idiomatic: Palace women repudiated Confucian doctrine and ministers spurned Jia Yi’s memorials—so belted scholars groaned aloud, even Liu Xiang and Dong Zhongshu struggling to hold their peace.

sentences.zh: 炎漢中興，明皇帝即位，表圭景而陳《清廟》，樹槐陰而疏璧流；

translations.literal: When fiery Han revived and Emperor Ming ascended the throne, he displayed the jade tablet’s shadow and presented “The Pure Temple”; planted catalpa shade and opened out jade-green currents;
translations.idiomatic: After Han’s revival, Emperor Ming took the throne: he read the sundial’s shadow and staged “The Pure Temple”; spread catalpa shade and let ritual currents shimmer like jade;

sentences.zh: 祀光武於明堂，以配上帝；

translations.literal: he sacrificed to Guangwu in the Bright Hall, pairing him with High God;
translations.idiomatic: offered Guangwu in the Bright Hall as counterpart to the Supreme Lord;

sentences.zh: 召桓榮於太學，袒而割牲；

translations.literal: summoned Huan Rong to the Imperial Academy, baring shoulder as he cut the victim;
translations.idiomatic: called Huan Rong to the academy and, shoulder bare, slew the sacrificial beast;

sentences.zh: 濟濟焉，皇皇焉，有足觀者。

translations.literal: grand indeed, august indeed—there was much worth seeing.
translations.idiomatic: the spectacle was stately, radiant with dignity—altogether worth beholding.

translations.literal: From that time onward, ritual and music grew ever richer.
translations.idiomatic: Afterward ritual observances and musical performance grew steadily more elaborate.

sentences.zh: 永平三年，官之司樂，改名大予，式揚典禮，旁求圖讖，道鄰《雅》《頌》，事邇中和。

translations.literal: In the third year of Yongping, the office in charge of music was renamed Grand Yu; it modeled canonical ceremony, gathered charts and prophecies on every side, aligned itself with the elegance of the Odes and Hymns, and kept close to the doctrine of harmonious equilibrium.
translations.idiomatic: In Yongping 3 the bureau of music became the Grand Yu office; it showcased classical liturgy, canvassed charts and omens, hugged the tone of the “Ya” and “Song,” and stayed tethered to the ideal of centered harmony.

sentences.zh: 其有五方之樂者，則所謂「大樂九變，天神可得而禮」也。

translations.literal: Where there is music of the five quarters, this is what is meant by “the Grand Music shifts through nine transformations, and spirits of Heaven may then receive sacrifice.”
translations.idiomatic: The five-direction ensemble embodies the saying, “When the Grand Music completes its nine mutations, celestial spirits may be feasted by ritual.”

sentences.zh: 其有宗廟之樂者，則所謂「肅雍和鳴，先祖是聽」者也。

translations.literal: Where there is ancestral-temple music, this is what is meant by “solemn harmony rings out, and the founding ancestors listen.”
translations.idiomatic: Temple pieces answer to the line, “Solemn concord sounds together, and the primal ancestors bend ear to it.”

sentences.zh: 其有社稷之樂者，則所謂「琴瑟擊鼓，以迓田祖」者也。

translations.literal: Where there is worship of soil and grain, this is what is meant by “zithers and drums strike up to welcome the field ancestor.”
translations.idiomatic: Music for the altars of soil and grain matches the verse, “With zither and drum they greet the lord of the furrows.”

sentences.zh: 其有辟雍之樂者，則所謂「移風易俗，莫善於樂」者也。

translations.literal: Where there is Yongyon academy music, this is what is meant by “to shift custom and improve morals, nothing surpasses music.”
translations.idiomatic: Music for the royal academy echoes the maxim, “Nothing reforms manners like music.”

sentences.zh: 其有黃門之樂者，則所謂「宴樂群臣，蹲蹲舞我」者也。

translations.literal: Where there is music of the Yellow Gate, this is what is meant by “feasting assembled ministers, stamping our dance in rhythm.”
translations.idiomatic: Palace banquet ensembles illustrate how one “feasts the throng of ministers while dancers stamp in neat rings.”

sentences.zh: 其有短簫之樂者，則所謂「王師大捷，令軍中凱歌」者也。

translations.literal: Where there is short-reed music, this is what is meant by “when the royal army wins decisively, order victory songs inside the host.”
translations.idiomatic: The shrill reed bands accompany the rule that after a great triumph the army must thunder victory songs.

sentences.zh: 魏武挾天子而令諸侯，思一戎而匡九服，時逢吞滅，憲章咸蕩。

translations.literal: While Wei Wu held the Son of Heaven hostage and commanded the lords, he wished one campaign to set right the nine circuits; in an age of annexation, statutes and models alike collapsed.
translations.idiomatic: Cao Cao, clutching the emperor to command the warlords, dreamed of a single expedition that would reorder the nine provinces; amid universal swallowing up, laws and precedents alike dissolved.

sentences.zh: 及削平劉表，始獲杜夔，揚鼙總幹，式遵前記。

translations.literal: Once he had crushed Liu Biao, he at last acquired Du Kui; drums were raised and shields grasped to follow ancient records.
translations.idiomatic: After Liu Biao fell, he finally gained Du Kui; drumheads sounded and dancers seized shields as old manuals prescribed.

sentences.zh: 三祖紛綸，咸工篇什，聲歌雖有損益，愛玩在乎雕章。

translations.literal: The three ancestors busied themselves one after another, all adept at composing verse; though songs gained or lost detail, their fondness lay in polishing phrases.
translations.idiomatic: Three successive Wei rulers threw themselves into verse; although tunes shifted in ornament, their delight rested in carved rhetoric.

sentences.zh: 是以王粲等各造新詩，抽其藻思，吟詠神靈，讚揚來饗。

translations.literal: Therefore Wang Can and others each fashioned new poems, drawing forth ornate conceits, chanting to the spirits and praising those who came to feast.
translations.idiomatic: Hence Wang Can and his fellows drafted fresh lyrics, spinning elaborate images to hymn the spirits and celebrate divine guests.

sentences.zh: 武皇帝采漢魏之遺范，覽景文之垂則，鼎鼐唯新，前音不改。

translations.literal: Emperor Wu of Jin adopted Han and Wei survivals, surveyed the lasting norms left by Jing and Wen, renewed the tripod vessels of state, yet left earlier musical substance unchanged.
translations.idiomatic: Jin’s Emperor Wu took Han–Wei patterns as his mold, reviewed precedents from the Simas Jing and Wen, replaced the ritual vessels, yet kept the older musical substance intact.

sentences.zh: 泰始九年，光祿大夫荀勖始作古尺，以調聲韻，仍以張華等所制高文，陳諸下管。

translations.literal: In the ninth year of Taishi, Minister Guanglu Xun Xu first fashioned ancient foot-rules to regulate modes and pitches, then still employed the lofty compositions by Zhang Hua and others, presenting them beneath the pipes.
translations.idiomatic: Taishi 9 saw Minister Xun Xu cast archaic measuring rods to tune intervals, then parade the majestic pieces Zhang Hua’s circle had written beneath the standing pipes.

sentences.zh: 永嘉之亂，伶官既減，曲台宣榭，咸變汙萊。

translations.literal: When the Yongjia turmoil struck, music officers were decimated; Terrace of Patterns and leaf-screened galleries alike sank into weed-choked wastes.
translations.idiomatic: The Yongjia disaster wiped out entire corps of musicians; Pattern Terrace and shuttered galleries alike turned to muddy ruin.

sentences.zh: 雖復《象舞》歌工，自胡歸晉，至於孤竹之管，雲和之瑟，空桑之琴，泗濱之磬，其能備者，百不一焉。

translations.literal: Though dancers for the “Elephant” dance and singing craftsmen returned from the northern tribes to Jin, as for Guzhu pipes, Yunhe zithers, hollow-sang lutes, and Siban chimes, scarcely one ensemble in a hundred remained complete.
translations.idiomatic: Even after “Elephant” dancers and choristers came south from the Hu domains, sets pairing Guzhu flutes, Yunhe zithers, hollow-sang lutes, and Siban stones survived intact perhaps once in a hundred cases.

sentences.zh: 夫人受天地之靈，蘊菁華之氣，剛柔遞用，哀樂分情。

translations.literal: Human beings receive the subtle powers of Heaven and Earth and harbor the condensed essence of brilliant vigor; hardness and softness alternate in application, grief and joy divide the feelings.
translations.idiomatic: People inherit Heaven and Earth’s spiritual charge and store its distilled brilliance; yielding and firm forces trade places in turn, while sorrow and joy partition the heart.

sentences.zh: 經春陽而自喜，遇秋雕而不悅。

translations.literal: Passing through spring sunshine they rejoice of themselves; meeting autumn’s stripping frost they lose cheer.
translations.idiomatic: Spring sunlight lifts them without prompting; autumn’s frost chills their mood unbidden.

sentences.zh: 游乎金石之端，出乎管弦之外，因物遷逝，乘流不反。

translations.literal: They roam at the boundary of metal and stone, sail beyond strings and pipes; things shift with circumstance and time drifts downstream without turning back.
translations.idiomatic: They wander where bells and stones fade into silence and drift beyond strings and winds; as circumstance turns, feeling rides the current and never reverses.

sentences.zh: 是以楚王升輕軒于彭蠡，漢順聽鳴鳥于樊衢。

translations.literal: Thus the king of Chu boarded his light carriage by Peng Lake, and Emperor Shun of Han listened to singing birds along the lanes of Fan.
translations.idiomatic: So the Chu king raced his light car beside Pengli marsh, while Emperor Shundi of Han lingered over birdsong where Fan’s highways crossed.

sentences.zh: 聖人功成作樂，化平裁曲，乃揚節奏，以暢中和，飾其歡欣，止於哀思者也。

translations.literal: Therefore when sages complete their work they create music; when transformation is balanced they trim melodies—only then do they lift beats and measures to vent centered harmony, adorn joy, and halt at mourning-thought.
translations.idiomatic: So the sage, achievements sealed and customs evenly ruled, fashions music and trims tunes—raising rhythm to release inner equipoise, heightening delight yet stopping short of mere lament.

sentences.zh: 凡樂之道，五聲、八音、六律、十二管，為之綱紀雲。

translations.literal: As a general principle of music, the five notes, eight timbres, six pitch-standards, and twelve tubes form its guiding threads.
translations.idiomatic: The whole art hangs on five tones, eight instrumental families, six canonical pitches, and twelve pipes—the cords that bind it.

sentences.zh: 五聲：宮為君，宮之為言中也。

translations.literal: Of the five tones: gong is lord; “gong” means centrality.
translations.idiomatic: Among the five tones gong acts as sovereign; the word “gong” signifies the middle.

sentences.zh: 中和之道，無往而不理焉。

translations.literal: The doctrine of centered harmony applies everywhere without obstacle.
translations.idiomatic: Central equipoise reaches everywhere without hindrance.

sentences.zh: 商為臣，商之為言強也，謂金性之堅強也。

translations.literal: Shang is minister; “shang” means strength—it speaks of the stubborn hardness of metal’s nature.
translations.idiomatic: Shang stands for ministers; “shang” means strength, naming the unyielding temper of metal.

sentences.zh: 角為民，角之為言觸也，謂象諸陽氣觸物而生也。

translations.literal: Jue is common people; “jue” means striking—it images how yang qi brushes against things and brings them to life.
translations.idiomatic: Jue stands for the folk; “jue” means touch, picturing yang vitality brushing creatures until they stir into life.

sentences.zh: 徵為事，征之為言止也，言物盛則止也。

translations.literal: Zhi governs affairs; “zhi” means stopping—it says when things flourish they halt.
translations.idiomatic: Zhi oversees practical affairs; etymologically it suggests stopping—things halt once they reach fullness.

sentences.zh: 羽為物，羽之為言舒也，言陽氣將復，萬物孳育而舒生也。

translations.literal: Yu governs material bounty; “yu” means spreading—it says yang qi will return and the myriad things breed and ease into growth.
translations.idiomatic: Yu presides over goods and harvests; “yu” implies easeful stretch—yang will surge again and creatures multiply in relaxed expansion.

sentences.zh: 古人有言曰：「禮樂不可斯須去身。

translations.literal: The ancients had a saying: “Ritual and music must never leave one even for a moment.”
translations.idiomatic: The ancients warned that ritual and music must never be absent even for an instant.

translations.literal: ” Transforming superiors and shifting the good seems scarcely fast enough.
translations.idiomatic: They lift those above toward goodness as though racing something that cannot be overtaken.

sentences.zh: 是以聞其宮聲，使人溫良而寬大；

translations.literal: Therefore hearing the gong tone makes people warm, kindly, and magnanimous;
translations.idiomatic: Hearing gong inclines one toward warmth, kindness, and breadth of heart;

sentences.zh: 聞其商聲，使人方廉而好義；

translations.literal: hearing the shang tone makes people upright, incorrupt, and fond of righteousness;
translations.idiomatic: shang fosters square integrity and zeal for duty;

sentences.zh: 聞其角聲，使人惻隱而仁愛；

translations.literal: hearing the jue tone makes people compassionate and humane;
translations.idiomatic: jue stirs pity and humane care;

sentences.zh: 聞其徵聲，使人樂養而好施；

translations.literal: hearing the zhi tone makes people cherish nurturing others and delight in giving;
translations.idiomatic: zhi encourages fostering life and generous sharing;

sentences.zh: 聞其羽聲，使人恭儉而好禮。

translations.literal: hearing the yu tone makes people respectful, frugal, and observant of ritual.
translations.idiomatic: yu molds reverence, thrift, and punctilious courtesy.

translations.literal: The eight timbres are the winds of the eight directions.
translations.idiomatic: Each of the eight instrumental families answers to a directional wind.

translations.literal: The sound of Qian is stone; its wind is Bu Zhou.
translations.idiomatic: Qian correlates with stone and the Bu Zhou wind.

translations.literal: The sound of Kan is leather; its wind is Guang Mo.
translations.idiomatic: Kan pairs with leather drums and the Guang Mo blast.

translations.literal: The sound of Gen is gourd; its wind is Rong.
translations.idiomatic: Gen matches gourd pipes and the melting Rong breeze.

translations.literal: The sound of Zhen is bamboo; its wind is Ming Shu.
translations.idiomatic: Zhen aligns with bamboo flutes and the Ming Shu wind of dawn.

translations.literal: The sound of Xun is wood; its wind is Qing Ming.
translations.idiomatic: Xun belongs to wooden clappers and the clear Qing Ming air.

translations.literal: The sound of Li is silk; its wind is Jing.
translations.idiomatic: Li answers to silk strings and the bright Jing current.

translations.literal: The sound of Kun is clay; its wind is Liang.
translations.idiomatic: Kun corresponds to earthen instruments and the cool Liang draft.

translations.literal: The sound of Dui is metal; its wind is Chang He.
translations.idiomatic: Dui joins metal bells with the Chang He gale at the celestial gate.

sentences.zh: 陽六為律，謂黃鐘、太蔟、姑洗、蕤賓、夷則、無射；

translations.literal: The six yang pitches are called lu: Huangzhong, Taicu, Guxian, Ruibin, Yize, and Wuyi;
translations.idiomatic: Six yang tubes are the lu pitches—Huangzhong, Taicu, Guxian, Ruibin, Yize, Wuyi—

sentences.zh: 陰六為呂，謂大呂、應鐘、南呂、林鐘、仲呂、夾鐘：凡有十二，以配十二辰焉。

translations.literal: the six yin are called lu complement: Dalu, Yingzhong, Nanlu, Linzhong, Zhonglu, and Jiazhong—twelve in all, paired with the twelve earthly branches.
translations.idiomatic: while six yin tubes form the companion lu—Dalu, Yingzhong, Nanlu, Linzhong, Zhonglu, Jiazhong—twelve pipes matching the twelve chronograms.

sentences.zh: 律之為言法也，言陽氣施生各有法也；

translations.literal: “Lu” means pattern—it says yang qi’s nurturing thrust each follows a rule;
translations.idiomatic: “Lu” denotes pattern: each surge of yang unfolds by rule;

sentences.zh: 呂之為言助也，所以助成陽功也。

translations.literal: “lu complement” means assistance—it aids in completing yang’s achievement.
translations.idiomatic: the companion series “assists,” completing what yang begins.

sentences.zh: 正月之辰謂之寅，寅者津也，謂生物之津塗也。

translations.literal: The chronogram of the first month is called yin; “yin” means ford—it speaks of the ford-path along which creatures come forth.
translations.idiomatic: The first month’s branch is yin; the gloss calls it a ford—the channel along which life ferries into the world.

sentences.zh: 二月之辰名為卯，卯者茂也，言陽氣生而孳茂也。

translations.literal: The chronogram of the second month is named mao; “mao” means luxuriance—it says yang qi has sprouted and grows thick.
translations.idiomatic: The second month is mao; “luxuriance” catches how yang thickens into riotous growth.

sentences.zh: 三月之辰名為辰，辰者震也，謂時物盡震動而長也。

translations.literal: The chronogram of the third month is named chen; “chen” means quake—it says things at this season all tremble as they lengthen.
translations.idiomatic: Third month chen means shaking—everything shudders upward into lengthening shoots.

sentences.zh: 四月之辰謂為巳，巳者起也，物至此時畢盡而起也。

translations.literal: The chronogram of the fourth month is called si; “si” means rising—it says things by now have fully emerged and begun to ascend.
translations.idiomatic: Fourth month si signals ascent—creatures stand fully risen from the soil.

sentences.zh: 五月之辰謂為午，午者長也，大也，言物皆長大也。

translations.literal: The chronogram of the fifth month is called wu; “wu” means growing great—it says things all attain large size.
translations.idiomatic: Fifth month wu stresses swelling bulk—forms reach mature size.

sentences.zh: 六月之辰謂之未，未者味也，言時萬物向成，有滋味也。

translations.literal: The chronogram of the sixth month is called wei; “wei” means flavor—it says the myriad things incline toward completion and begin to taste ripe.
translations.idiomatic: Sixth month wei is “flavor,” when crops edge toward harvest and savor fills the grain.

sentences.zh: 七月之辰謂為申，申者身也，言時萬物身體皆成就也。

translations.literal: The chronogram of the seventh month is called shen; “shen” means body—it says the myriad things’ bodies are all accomplished.
translations.idiomatic: Seventh month shen marks completeness of bodily form in field and forest.

sentences.zh: 八月之辰謂為酉，酉者緧也，謂時物皆綇縮也。

translations.literal: The chronogram of the eighth month is called you; “you” means binding—it says things at this season all curl inward and shrink.
translations.idiomatic: Eighth month you speaks of tightening—growth binds inward and slack tissues contract.

sentences.zh: 九月之辰謂為戌，戌者滅也，謂時物皆衰滅也。

translations.literal: The chronogram of the ninth month is called xu; “xu” means extinction—it says things at this season all wither away.
translations.idiomatic: Ninth month xu is extinction—the surge of life visibly gutters out.

sentences.zh: 十月之辰謂為亥，亥者劾也，言時陰氣劾殺萬物也。

translations.literal: The chronogram of the tenth month is called hai; “hai” means restraining—it says yin qi at this season checks and slays the myriad things.
translations.idiomatic: Tenth month hai names restraint—yin clamps down and cuts life short.

sentences.zh: 十一月之辰謂為子，子者孳也，謂陽氣至此更孳生也。

translations.literal: The chronogram of the eleventh month is called zi; “zi” means breeding anew—it says yang qi reaches this point and breeds again.
translations.idiomatic: Eleventh month zi promises fresh breeding—yang gathers for another birth pulse.

sentences.zh: 十二月之辰謂為醜，醜者紐也，言終始之際，以紐結為名也。

translations.literal: The chronogram of the twelfth month is called chou; “chou” means knot—it speaks of the hinge between ending and beginning, named for tying tight.
translations.idiomatic: Twelfth month chou is the knot—year-end and year-begin latch together like a closed circle.

sentences.zh: 十一月之管謂之黃鐘，黃者，陰陽之中色也。

translations.literal: The tube of the eleventh month is called Huangzhong; “huang” is the neutral color between yin and yang.
translations.idiomatic: The pipe tuned to the eleventh month is Huangzhong; yellow names the balanced hue between yin and yang.

sentences.zh: 天有六氣，地有五才，而天地數畢焉。

translations.literal: Heaven has six vapors, Earth five materials—thus the numerology of Heaven and Earth is complete.
translations.idiomatic: Heaven wields six qi, Earth five elements—together their tallies close the cosmic account.

sentences.zh: 或曰，冬至德氣為土，土色黃，故曰黃鐘。

translations.literal: Some say: at the winter solstice the virtue-current is earth; earth’s color is yellow—hence Huangzhong.
translations.idiomatic: Another gloss claims winter solstice’s virtue-climate belongs to earth, whose color is yellow—thus the name Huangzhong.

sentences.zh: 正月之管謂為太蔟，蔟者蔟也，謂萬物隨于陽氣太蔟而生也。

translations.literal: The tube of the first month is called Taicu; “cu” means clustering—it says the myriad things follow swelling yang and cluster into life.
translations.idiomatic: The first month’s pipe is Taicu; “cluster” describes creatures massing as yang billows.

sentences.zh: 三月之管名為姑洗，姑洗者：姑，枯也；

translations.literal: The tube of the third month is named Guxian; concerning Guxian: gu means withered;
translations.idiomatic: Third month’s tube is Guxian; “gu” glosses as dry stalk—

sentences.zh: 洗，濯也，謂物生新潔，洗除其枯，改柯易葉也。

translations.literal: xian means washing—it says things freshly born are cleansed, scrubbing away the withered husks and exchanging stems for new leaves.
translations.idiomatic: “xian” means rinse—new shoots scour off dead bark and trade old stems for fresh foliage.

sentences.zh: 五月之管名為蕤賓，葳蕤，垂下貌也；

translations.literal: The tube of the fifth month is named Ruibin; “ruibin” describes luxuriant hanging;
translations.idiomatic: Fifth month Ruibin pictures lush pendulous growth—

sentences.zh: 賓，敬也，謂時陽氣下降，陰氣始起，相賓敬也。

translations.literal: bin means reverence—it says yang qi sinks while yin qi first arises; the two salute each other.
translations.idiomatic: while “guest” implies reverence as yang dips and yin rises to greet it like a respected visitor.

sentences.zh: 七月之管名為夷則，夷，平也；

translations.literal: The tube of the seventh month is named Yize; yi means leveling;
translations.idiomatic: Seventh month Yize begins with “even”—

sentences.zh: 則，法也，謂萬物將成，平均皆有法則也。

translations.literal: ze means pattern—it says the myriad things will achieve fullness and each possesses a norm.
translations.idiomatic: then “rule”: harvest looms and every creature evens into lawful proportion.

sentences.zh: 九月之管名為無射，射者出也，言時陽氣上升，萬物收藏無復出也。

translations.literal: The tube of the ninth month is named Wuyi; the gloss takes “shoot” as “issue forth”—yang qi mounts while the myriad things are stored inward and nothing further issues outward.
translations.idiomatic: Ninth month Wuyi reads “discharge”: yang still climbs, yet creatures seal harvest away and nothing thrusts out again.

sentences.zh: 十二月之管名為大呂，呂者助也，謂陽氣方之，陰氣助也。

translations.literal: The tube of the twelfth month is named Dalu; “lu” means assistance—it says yang qi is just arriving while yin qi assists.
translations.idiomatic: Twelfth month Dalu keeps “assist”: yang flickers back while yin lends stabilizing support.

sentences.zh: 十月之管名為應鐘，應者和也，謂歲功皆成，應和陽功，收而聚之也。

translations.literal: The tube of the tenth month is named Yingzhong; ying means resonance—it says the year’s work is finished; responding to yang’s merit, it gathers everything in.
translations.idiomatic: Tenth month Yingzhong’s “answer” marks harvest sealed—yang’s labor receives answering chorus as energies fold inward.

sentences.zh: 八月之管名為南呂，南者任也，謂時物皆秀，有懷任之象也。

translations.literal: The tube of the eighth month is named Nanlu; nan means burden—it says things at this season all hold seed, bearing the pregnant shape of what comes next.
translations.idiomatic: Eighth month Nanlu reads “shoulder”—stalks bend under grain already swelling toward next spring’s sowing.

sentences.zh: 六月之管名為林鐘，林者茂也，謂時物茂盛於野也。

translations.literal: The tube of the sixth month is named Linzhong; “lin” means luxuriance—it says things at this season grow lush across the wilds.
translations.idiomatic: Sixth month’s pipe is Linzhong—“forest-thick” evokes rank growth carpeting the open countryside.

sentences.zh: 四月之管名為仲呂者，呂，助也，謂陽氣盛長，陰助成功也。

translations.literal: The tube of the fourth month is named Zhonglu; “lu” means assistance—it says yang qi swells and lengthens while yin assists and completes the work.
translations.idiomatic: Fourth month answers to Zhonglu; “assist” catches how swelling yang still needs yin’s steady help to finish forming things.

sentences.zh: 二月之管名為夾鐘者，夾，佐也，謂時物尚未盡出，陰德佐陽而出物也。

translations.literal: The tube of the second month is named Jiazhong; “jia” means flank-support—it says creatures are not yet fully emerged, and yin virtue aids yang so things break outward.
translations.idiomatic: The second month names the pipe Jiazhong; reading jia as flank-support, yin braces yang while new growth still hesitates beneath the soil.

sentences.zh: 漢自東京大亂，絕無金石之樂，樂章亡缺，不可復知。

translations.literal: From Han’s Eastern Capital era of great turmoil onward, metal and stone instruments vanished utterly; musical chapters were lost or defective and could not be recovered.
translations.idiomatic: After Luoyang sank into chaos, Han possessed no bronze bells or lithophones; scores rotted away beyond reconstruction.

sentences.zh: 及魏武平荊州，獲漢雅樂郎河南杜夔，能識舊法，以為軍謀祭酒，使創定雅樂。

translations.literal: When Wei Wu pacified Jing Province, he captured Du Kui of Henan, the Han Master of Ritual Music, who still understood the old methods; Wei Wu appointed him Army Counsel Superintendent and ordered him to recreate and fix ritual music.
translations.idiomatic: Cao Cao’s conquest of Jingzhou yielded Du Kui, the Eastern Han’s keeper of court pitch; knowing antique procedure, he became Libationer for Military Counsel and received orders to codify classical sound anew.

sentences.zh: 時又有散騎侍郎鄧靜、尹商善訓雅樂，歌師尹胡能歌宗廟郊祀之曲，舞師馮肅、服養曉知先代諸舞，夔悉總領之。

translations.literal: At the same time Gentlemen for Imperial Household Cadence Deng Jing and Yin Shang excelled at drilling ritual music; singer Yin Hu could perform ancestral-temple and suburban-sacrifice airs; dance masters Feng Su and Fu Yang understood former dynasties’ dances—Du Kui supervised them all.
translations.idiomatic: Meanwhile Deng Jing and Yin Shang, household advisers, drilled choristers in ritual repertoire; Yin Hu sang suburban and temple hymns; Feng Su and Fu Yang staged archaic dances—every troupe answered to Du Kui.

sentences.zh: 遠詳經籍，近采故事，考會古樂，始設軒懸鐘磬。

translations.literal: Consulting distant classics and adopting recent precedents, they collated ancient music and first arranged the suspended bells and chimes of the curtained gallery.
translations.idiomatic: They combed canon and recent statute, reconciled archaic pitch systems, and debuted the bell-and-stone arrays hung along three sides.

sentences.zh: 而黃初中柴玉、左延年之徒，復以新聲被寵，改其聲韻。

translations.literal: Yet during Huangchu, men such as Chai Yu and Zuo Yannian, favored for novelty, again altered modes and resonance.
translations.idiomatic: Yet in Huangchu favorites like Chai Yu and Zuo Yannian won patronage with fashionable tunes and bent the scales anew.

sentences.zh: 及武帝受命之初，百度草創。

translations.literal: When Emperor Wu first received Heaven’s charge, every regulation was still rough-hewn.
translations.idiomatic: At the outset of Jin’s mandate, institutions existed only in embryo.

sentences.zh: 泰始二年，詔郊祀明堂禮樂權用魏儀，遵周室肇稱殷禮之義，但改樂章而已，使傅玄為之詞雲。

translations.literal: In the second year of Taishi an edict declared that suburban rites, the Bright Hall, ritual, and music should provisionally follow Wei ceremony—honoring Zhou’s precedent of initially labeling rituals Yin—except that hymn texts alone were replaced, assigning Fu Xuan to compose the lyrics.
translations.idiomatic: Taishi 2 ordered suburban and Bright Hall liturgy to borrow Wei forms—echoing Zhou’s habit of calling early rituals Shang-style—while swapping only the hymn lyrics, commissioned from Fu Xuan.

translations.literal: Song for the Evening Victim at Suburban Sacrifice to Heaven and Earth and the Five Quarters
translations.idiomatic: Evening Offering Hymn: Five-Direction Heaven-and-Earth Suburban Rite

translations.literal: Heaven decreed the Jin house—grave, radiant, and bright.
translations.idiomatic: Heaven pronounced its mandate upon Jin—solemn, luminous, august.

translations.literal: We rise early and retire late, reverently serving the High Spirits.
translations.idiomatic: Night and day we hurry to attend the supreme numina with awe.

translations.literal: Ever may They lodge here for this season’s observance; we carry through to completion what we begin.
translations.idiomatic: May the spirits habitually pause among us this hour; we press the rite to its finished fulfillment.

translations.literal: We present the black bull; at dusk we advance the victim.
translations.idiomatic: Black steer stands ready; at vesper hour we bring the offerings forward.

translations.literal: Through ennobling virtue we fashion music—spirits and earthly gods bend ear.
translations.idiomatic: Music shaped by towering virtue reaches divine and chthonic powers alike.

translations.literal: Song for Welcoming and Sending the Spirits at Suburban Sacrifice to Heaven and Earth and the Five Quarters
translations.idiomatic: Processional Hymn: Welcoming and Speeding the Spirits (Five-Direction Suburban Rite)

translations.literal: How Emperor Wen flourished—quieting the four quarters day by day.
translations.idiomatic: King Wen’s pattern glows; his quiet virtue pacifies every quarter.

translations.literal: Forever may we guard it, never resting morning or night.
translations.idiomatic: We vow perpetual guardianship, knowing no ease from dawn to dusk.

translations.literal: The mandate spanning bright Heaven—High God is sovereign.
translations.idiomatic: Bright Heaven’s charge rests august; the Supreme Lord reigns above.

translations.literal: Glad music piles high in offering—spirit blessings blaze auspiciously.
translations.idiomatic: Festive tones heap the altar; numinous fortune flames forth in glory.

translations.literal: Spirits descend to lodge—boundless felicity is theirs.
translations.idiomatic: Divine guests descend to tarry; happiness knows no edge.

translations.literal: Song for Feasting Heaven and Earth at Suburban Sacrifice to the Five Quarters
translations.idiomatic: Communion Hymn: Five-Direction Heaven-and-Earth Banquet

translations.literal: Heaven blesses Jin—the charge is fresh.
translations.idiomatic: Heaven keeps Jin alive; its mandate gleams anew.

translations.literal: Receiving the finale from Wei, they embrace all the black-haired people.
translations.idiomatic: Taking Wei’s conclusion as prelude, they fold every household under rule.

translations.literal: Offering spreads to august Heaven; harmony clasps the hundred gods.
translations.idiomatic: Smoke rises to mighty Heaven; every god gathers in concord.

translations.literal: Brilliantly manifest is the legacy left behind—pure is its virtue.
translations.idiomatic: Their legacy blazes undimmed—virtue distilled to flawless clarity.

translations.literal: They feast upon the black ox; thus they inaugurate the burnt offering.
translations.idiomatic: They partake of the dark-hided steer; thus kindling inaugurates the smoky prayer.

translations.literal: Spirits arrive in ranks—fortune and salary converge.
translations.idiomatic: Numina crowd to attend; blessings and stipends bunch together.

translations.literal: Time moves with prudent awe—Haotian’s Son upholds it.
translations.idiomatic: The seasons march in reverent caution; the Son of Heaven sustains that rhythm.

translations.literal: Heaven’s aid favors Jin—the myriad subjects crown it.
translations.idiomatic: Providential favor settles on Jin; commoners alike pledge allegiance.

translations.literal: We fear Heaven’s majesty and respectfully hand down human seasons.
translations.idiomatic: We tremble before celestial sternness and reverently publish the farming calendar.

translations.literal: Brilliantly they carry forward—thought prolongs their caution.
translations.idiomatic: Glory inherited and glory sustained—reflection stretches their vigilance.

translations.literal: The royal pivot stands established—every task shines with success.
translations.idiomatic: Once the imperial pole plants firm, every undertaking gleams ordered peace.

translations.literal: Would that night and day never slack—such is Jin’s felicity.
translations.idiomatic: Grant us diligence without cease—the very blessing of our Jin age.

translations.literal: King Wen alone serves as spouse-partner to High Heaven.
translations.idiomatic: Emperor Wen pairs worthily with Heaven on high.

translations.literal: He soothed the four seas and guarded years of peace.
translations.idiomatic: He quieted the realm within four shores and kept healthy harvest years.

translations.literal: Ah, how far-shining—freely he brings calm to the folk.
translations.idiomatic: O that spreading radiance—effortlessly he steadies every household.

translations.literal: Thus statutes were framed and ritual canons trimmed.
translations.idiomatic: Thus codes took shape and ceremonial chapters were polished.

translations.literal: Setting the people’s pole-star—nothing fails to draw sustenance from the beginning.
translations.idiomatic: They fixed the lodestar for the people—nothing lacks its root in primordial bounty.

translations.literal: May posterity flourish forever—ever shall we guard this legacy.
translations.idiomatic: May heirs flourish without end—we vow eternal guardianship of their gift.

translations.literal: Evening Victim Song for Suburban Rites and the Bright Hall to Heaven and Earth
translations.idiomatic: Evening Offering Hymn: Round-and-Square Altars and Bright Hall

translations.literal: How great is Jin—its virtue strides with the seasons.
translations.idiomatic: Lofty stands Jin; its power tracks the turning year.

translations.literal: Receiving the mandate from Heaven, its radiance succors myriad states.
translations.idiomatic: Heaven’s finale passes to them; their brilliance nurses ten thousand domains.

translations.literal: Once myriad states feel that radiance, the gods fix auspicious signs.
translations.idiomatic: When every region drinks that light, spirits seal propitious omens.

translations.literal: Reverent at suburban sacrifice—they serve High Sovereign above.
translations.idiomatic: Suburban offerings unfold in awe; they wait upon the highest sovereign.

translations.literal: Serving High Sovereign—every blessing arrives.
translations.idiomatic: Serving that sovereign—every blessing crowds home.

translations.literal: Towering are the founding fathers—worthy mates for Heaven.
translations.idiomatic: Majestic ancestors align worthily with Heaven’s pole.

translations.literal: Fine victims bring no mere satiety—fragrant virtue is the feast.
translations.idiomatic: Splendid oxen do not merely fill the belly—virtue’s aroma is the offering.

translations.literal: Receiving Heaven’s protection—their divine transformation fills the four quarters.
translations.idiomatic: Heaven’s shield lies upon them; spiritual transformation washes the four corners.

translations.literal: Song for the Descent of Spirits at Suburban Rites and the Bright Hall to Heaven and Earth
translations.idiomatic: Descent Hymn: Spirits at Round-and-Square Altars and Bright Hall

translations.literal: Radiant, mighty Great Jin answers Heaven’s bright omens.
translations.idiomatic: Resplendent Great Jin catches Heaven’s glittering portents.

translations.literal: The Two Emperors stride in virtue and broadcast this redoubled glory.
translations.idiomatic: Two sage-kings march in accumulated power, doubling that luminous legacy.

translations.literal: Our sovereign received the charge—embracing the myriad regions.
translations.idiomatic: Our emperor took Heaven’s writ—cradling every province within.

translations.literal: Suburban offerings pair worthy helpers—ritual and music resound in splendor.
translations.idiomatic: Suburban hosts join paired spirits—music and rite shine in perfect array.

translations.literal: Spirits rejoice in the banquet—ancestors reign supreme.
translations.idiomatic: Gods delight in the feast; forefathers hold sovereign seats.

translations.literal: May posterity thrive—protection knows no boundary.
translations.idiomatic: May heirs flourish forever—guardianship never finds its edge.

translations.literal: Song for Feasting the Spirit at the Heaven Suburb
translations.idiomatic: Communion Hymn: Celestial Suburban Altar

translations.literal: We array the great tai altar—we honor the August Spirit.
translations.idiomatic: The vast tai terrace lies ordered; we reverence the sovereign god.

translations.literal: Essential energies stir—the hundred numina arrive as guests.
translations.idiomatic: Refined breath moves; every spirit presents itself as honored guest.

translations.literal: Vermilion flame is hoarded; fragrant fuel coils about.
translations.idiomatic: Crimson fire nests within; aromatic kindling winds through the pyre.

translations.literal: Purple vapor drifts; it caps the green clouds.
translations.idiomatic: Indigo smoke wanders; it crowns the azure clouds.

translations.literal: The god’s substance—never fixed in any shape.
translations.idiomatic: Divinity’s body owns no single silhouette.

translations.literal: Vast without quarter—shadowy, yet limpid.
translations.idiomatic: Boundless beyond direction—dim, yet crystalline.

translations.literal: When the god approaches—glory and light flare.
translations.idiomatic: At the spirit’s advent—radiance flares like dawn.

translations.literal: Nothing heard with ear—nothing seen as omen.
translations.idiomatic: No sound strikes the ear—no image meets the eye.

translations.literal: When the god reaches us—every heart lifts in joy.
translations.idiomatic: When the deity arrives—each breast thrills with reverent gladness.

translations.literal: Numinous cool agrees within—stirring what lingers in our hearts.
translations.idiomatic: Ghostly clarity harmonizes inside—rousing the depths of our hearts.

translations.literal: When the god sits—joy is shared alike.
translations.idiomatic: Once the spirit is seated—delight runs common through the hall.

translations.literal: Moist clouds soar; transforming winds spread.
translations.idiomatic: Blessed rains ride cloud; edifying breezes unfurl.

translations.literal: Fine music plays—the patterned tones hold center.
translations.idiomatic: Harmony rises; civil sound occupies the middle voice.

translations.literal: Eight timbres chime as one—the god listens.
translations.idiomatic: Eight instrumental families accord—the deity bends ear.

translations.literal: All modes align—fragrance mingles everywhere.
translations.idiomatic: Every mode locks in step—sweet savor suffuses the air.

translations.literal: We boil and roast victims; we raise jade goblets.
translations.idiomatic: Steaming flesh steams; jade cups lift in toast.

translations.literal: The god delights in the feast—our smoky offering pleases.
translations.idiomatic: The spirit joys at the banquet—our burnt incense satisfies.

translations.literal: Protect Great Jin—send down blessings thick as rain.
translations.idiomatic: Shield mighty Jin—pour blessings in lavish sheets.

translations.literal: Raise the capital—extend through the four seas.
translations.idiomatic: Exalt the royal capital—push virtue across four oceans.

translations.literal: Guard Heaven’s years—span Earth’s reckoning.
translations.idiomatic: Preserve Heaven-allotted age—track Earth’s eternal tally.

translations.literal: Song for Feasting the Spirit at the Earth Suburb
translations.idiomatic: Communion Hymn: Terrestrial Suburban Altar

translations.literal: We array great She—we await the royal Earth god.
translations.idiomatic: The mighty She altar stands straight; we await the august soil deity.

translations.literal: Crowds of gods respond—hosts of spirits keep ritual demeanor.
translations.idiomatic: Legions of gods stir; companies of ghosts observe ordained bearing.

translations.literal: Shade offerings are set—auspicious rites unfold.
translations.idiomatic: Yin-side offerings rise; blessed ceremony proceeds.

translations.literal: Night nears its depth—yet the hour does not shift.
translations.idiomatic: Midnight crowds close—still the appointed hour lingers.

translations.literal: The god’s substance—without shape or image.
translations.idiomatic: Earth’s numen owns no portrait—no borrowed likeness.

translations.literal: Hidden in mighty silence—penetrating vast obscurity.
translations.idiomatic: Veiled in deepest stillness—threading boundless murk.

translations.literal: When the god emerges—hovering as though half-seen.
translations.idiomatic: When the deity steps forth—a haze suggests its presence.

translations.literal: Numina know no distance—they are mother to all under Heaven.
translations.idiomatic: Spirits ignore mileage—they nurse everything beneath the sky.

translations.literal: When the god draws near—it trails trails of light.
translations.idiomatic: When it approaches—light-shadows trail behind.

translations.literal: Bright as though present—yet ending in deep gloom.
translations.idiomatic: Luminous as if tangibly here—yet sinking into twilight dim.

translations.literal: When the god arrives—every face blooms glad.
translations.idiomatic: When the spirit reaches us—each countenance opens in joy.

translations.literal: Dances image virtue—songs complete the pattern.
translations.idiomatic: Dance bodies forth virtue; song finishes the design.

translations.literal: Once the god is seated—delight is shared in ease.
translations.idiomatic: Seated, the spirit shares untroubled pleasure with us.

translations.literal: Blessing rains deploy—transforming clouds spread.
translations.idiomatic: Kind rains unfurl; instructive clouds mantle the fields.

translations.literal: Music shifts through eight turns—teaching’s voice spreads abroad.
translations.idiomatic: Eight transformations roll the tune—moral instruction scatters wide.

translations.literal: Things all thrive—the god takes joy.
translations.idiomatic: Creatures prosper alike—the deity finds delight.

translations.literal: Vessels cleansed—attendants stand rigid.
translations.idiomatic: Regalia purified—servers hold disciplined stance.

translations.literal: Jade cups advance—all kneel in solemn hush.
translations.idiomatic: Jade goblets rise—every courtier bows in muted awe.

translations.literal: We feast fine livestock—we savor fragrant virtue.
translations.idiomatic: We banquet on choice herds—we inhale virtue’s perfume.

translations.literal: Fortune rests on Jin—reaching every creature.
translations.idiomatic: Blessing settles on Jin—spilling over all that lives.

translations.literal: Spilling past nine soils—it pierces the celestial court.
translations.idiomatic: Overflowing ninefold realms—it penetrates the gates of Heaven.

translations.literal: Protect myriad longevities—extend hundred-million spans.
translations.idiomatic: Guard ten thousand years of life—prolong innumerable ages.

translations.literal: Song for Feasting the Spirit at the Bright Hall
translations.idiomatic: Communion Hymn: Bright Hall

translations.literal: From the first framing of the Bright Hall—offerings never slack.
translations.idiomatic: Since first they laid out the Bright Hall, sacrifice knows no neglect.

translations.literal: Oh glorious fierce Father—his brilliance pairs High God.
translations.idiomatic: How bright our martial royal father—his splendor mates with Heaven’s sovereign.

translations.literal: August is High God—already lofty, already exalted.
translations.idiomatic: High God towers sublime—lifted high, lifted vast.

translations.literal: The sage Father matches Him—bright virtue shines abroad.
translations.idiomatic: Our sage father stands as counterpart—lucent power floods every quarter.

translations.literal: Within the realm all offices stand in awe—myriad regions arrive to sacrifice.
translations.idiomatic: Every soil attends its duty; ten thousand quarters come bearing offerings.

translations.literal: Ever may They lodge here for this season—protect the throne through endless ages.
translations.idiomatic: May spirits pause by custom’s hour—shield the mandate age on age.

translations.literal: Evening Victim Song for the Ancestral Shrine
translations.idiomatic: Evening Offering Hymn: Ancestral Temple

translations.literal: At dusk we ready our victim—ah, how reverent our halt.
translations.idiomatic: We prepare the steer at vesper—oh the awe that stays our steps.

translations.literal: Fine livestock arrive at proper hour—we supply this communion feast.
translations.idiomatic: Choice herds align with the appointed hour—we spread this banquet offering.

translations.literal: Spirits mirror such sincerity—great and abundant, They savor it.
translations.idiomatic: The gods scan their earnest hearts—rich portions win divine relish.

sentences.zh: 祖考降饗，以虞孝孫之心。

translations.idiomatic: Temple Stair Hymn: Yuzhang Prefect Lord

translations.idiomatic: Rank on rank of lords attend—they joint-host autumn and winter rites.

translations.literal: The communion knows no fault—fortune rains thickly down.

translations.idiomatic: Temple Stair Hymn: Yingchuan Prefect Lord

translations.literal: Ah, remote queen mother—she truly holds Heaven’s charge.
translations.idiomatic: Far-shining queen mother—she indeed ministers for Heaven.

translations.literal: Manifest is royal ancestor—imperial blessing first arrives.
translations.idiomatic: Bright our royal founder—Heaven’s luck first settled here.

translations.literal: Root and branches flourish together—the foundation opens primal fortune.
translations.idiomatic: Trunk and twigs thrive alike—the base splits open Genesis fortune.

translations.literal: Their kindness knows no bound—may fortune-seat endure ten thousand years.
translations.idiomatic: Their mercy spans infinity—may the throne endure endless years.

translations.literal: Ascending Hymn for Lord of Capital Region Prefecture
translations.idiomatic: Temple Stair Hymn: Metropolitan Prefect Lord

translations.literal: Ah, our august grandfather—bright stands his peerless virtue.
translations.idiomatic: Lofty that royal grandfather—virtue gleams beyond compare.

sentences.zh: 商明清亮，匪競柔克，保乂命祐，基命惟則。

translations.literal: Judgment lucid, purity bright—not striving yet supple mastery—guarding order, commanding blessing—founding mandate rests in norms.
translations.idiomatic: Insight acute and clarity radiant—without quarrel yet mastering yielding strength—preserving peace and decreeing grace—the primal mandate roots in law.

translations.literal: Earnestly was born our sage ancestor—his radiance succored four states.
translations.idiomatic: From him sprang the sage founder—his brilliance nursed the four quarters.

translations.literal: Ascending Hymn for Emperor Xuan
translations.idiomatic: Temple Stair Hymn: Emperor Xuan

translations.literal: How radiant Emperor Xuan—sacred virtue revered and bright.
translations.idiomatic: Blazing royal ancestor Xuan—sagely power awe-full and clear.

translations.literal: He tirelessly spread virtue through four quarters—morning and night he stopped only in reverence.
translations.idiomatic: He poured transformation across the realm—rising early, retiring late in awe alone.

translations.literal: He unfolded civil instruction—he raised martial glory.
translations.idiomatic: He rolled out literary teaching—he brandished military might.

translations.literal: He steadied soil and grain—he enacted Heaven’s punishments.
translations.idiomatic: He squared altars of state—he executed Heaven’s sentences against rebels.

translations.literal: He opened the great enterprise—he founded the imperial base.
translations.idiomatic: He launched the mega-task—he laid the emperor’s footing.

translations.literal: He feared Heaven’s command—thereby guarding it for his age.
translations.idiomatic: He trembled at celestial decree—thus keeping faith with his times.

translations.literal: Ascending Hymn for Emperor Jing
translations.idiomatic: Temple Stair Hymn: Emperor Jing

translations.literal: Striving stands Emperor Jing—both discerning and wise.
translations.idiomatic: Intent Emperor Jing presses onward—clarifying and wise together.

translations.literal: All around they modeled solemn awe—only reverence, only dread.
translations.idiomatic: Every side echoed grave silence—nothing but awe, nothing but fear.

translations.literal: He carried Xuan’s legacy—aged and settled that merit.
translations.idiomatic: He picked up Xuan’s thread—aged its achievements firm.

translations.literal: He raised these splendid assistants—he twisted rope around those villains.
translations.idiomatic: He lifted worthy ministers—he bound rebel packs for judgment.

translations.literal: Awed they stood in office—yet the emperor daily labored on.
translations.idiomatic: Grave they stayed at post—the emperor himself never rested.

translations.literal: Such is Heaven’s charge—oh how august its silence.
translations.idiomatic: Such runs Heaven’s decree—oh how solemn its stillness.

translations.literal: Ascending Hymn for Emperor Wen
translations.idiomatic: Temple Stair Hymn: Emperor Wen

sentences.zh: 于皇時晉，允文文皇，聰明睿智，聖敬神武。

translations.literal: Oh great Jin of this hour—truly cultured Emperor Wen—acute hearing, keen sight, sage reverence, spirit-like martial poise.
translations.idiomatic: Hail Jin today—credibly cultured Emperor Wen—acute of ear and eye, holy in awe, godlike in arms.

translations.literal: Ten thousand skeins of rule—none he failed to thread—thus the throne stays clear.
translations.idiomatic: No tangled court thread escaped him—the realm stayed lucid under hand.

translations.literal: Snakes and boars defied command—thus he pacified them.
translations.idiomatic: Serpent-and-swine rebels flouted Heaven—thus he crushed them flat.

translations.literal: He softened those afar and bridled near—briefly selecting splendid worthies.
translations.idiomatic: He gentled distant tribes and steadied neighbors—swiftly elevating heroes.

translations.literal: He founded enterprise and handed down succession—merit matched august Heaven.
translations.idiomatic: He began the work and passed its warp—achievements rivaled bright Heaven.

translations.literal: Two Pieces: Songs for Feasting Spirits at the Ancestral Shrine
translations.idiomatic: Twin Communion Hymns: Ancestral Temple

translations.literal: They declare Jin the constant—communion follows seasonal order.
translations.idiomatic: They proclaim Jin the fixed offering—sacrifice tracks ritual seasons.

translations.literal: The lineage shrine pays deepest homage—ritual and music stand complete.
translations.idiomatic: Ancestors receive utmost reverence—music and ceremony rise together.

translations.literal: Whenever sacrifice draws near—all lands beneath Heaven hasten.
translations.idiomatic: Whenever offerings assemble—the whole realm within the seas races here.

translations.literal: Sacrificial goblets already set—clear ale already poured.
translations.idiomatic: Bronze beast cups stand filled—bright spirits already swim in jars.

translations.literal: Harmonizing broth joins them—delicacies arrive as due.
translations.idiomatic: Balanced stew accompanies—fine cuts pile as ordained.

translations.literal: Steam rises with ceaseless longing—moved by season, memories swell.
translations.idiomatic: Fragrant steam lifts endless grief—the hour stirs thoughts of forebears.

translations.literal: Ascending songs sound and dancers tread—the spirits rejoice in concord.
translations.idiomatic: Stair hymns rise and dancers stamp—the gods delight in harmony.

translations.literal: Ancestors arrive to inspect—They bless our kingdom house.
translations.idiomatic: Forefathers step among us—shield our dynastic hall.

translations.literal: Beneath wide Heaven none fail to praise.
translations.idiomatic: Under vast sky none withhold joyful praise.

translations.literal: Solemn stand those at post—crowded stand ministerial officers.
translations.idiomatic: Grave they hold their stations—dense ranks of ministers attend.

translations.literal: Four seas arrive to align—numinous bearing shows composed grace.
translations.idiomatic: Every shore sends delegations—spirit processions keep ritual poise.

sentences.zh: 鐘鼓振，管弦理，舞開元，歌永始，神胥樂兮！

translations.literal: Bells and drums quiver—pipes and strings align—dance opens Kaiyuan—song lifts Yongshi—the gods all rejoice!
translations.idiomatic: Bronze tolls shiver—reed banks tune—dance unveils Primordial Opening—chorus launches Eternal Beginning—every deity thrills with joy!

translations.literal: Solemn stand those at post—great and small ministers crowded.
translations.idiomatic: Awed they stay at station—hosts of officers crowd the ranks.

translations.literal: Young and old alike reverent—above and below observe ritual.
translations.idiomatic: Lesser and greater share awe—high and low keep courteous order.

sentences.zh: 理管弦，振鼓鐘，舞象德，歌詠功，神胥樂兮！

translations.literal: They tune pipes and strings—they rouse bells and drums—they dance virtue embodied—they chant merit wrought—the gods all rejoice!
translations.idiomatic: Wind instruments settle—bronze answers—dance bodies forth virtue—song tallies deeds—every spirit sings gladness!

translations.literal: Solemn stand those at post—many arrive in harmonious throng.
translations.idiomatic: Grave they fill the hall—hosts arrive in tranquil tide.

translations.literal: Solemn stands Son of Heaven—noble dukes flank him as aides.
translations.idiomatic: August the celestial king—paired by regional lords at side.

sentences.zh: 禮有儀，樂有則，舞象功，歌詠德，神胥樂兮！

translations.literal: Rite owns its forms—music owns its norms—dance figures merit—song chants virtue—the gods all rejoice!
translations.idiomatic: Ceremony keeps measure—music keeps rule—dance maps achievement—lyric praises power—every god laughs with pleasure!

sentences.zh: 杜夔傳舊雅樂四曲，一曰《鹿鳴》，二曰《騶虞》，三曰《伐檀》，四曰《文王》，皆古聲辭。

translations.literal: Du Kui transmitted former ritual music in four pieces—first “Deer Call,” second “Zouyu,” third “Cutting Sandalwood,” fourth “King Wen”—all antique tunes and texts.
translations.idiomatic: Du Kui handed down four classical chamber pieces—“Deer Call,” “Zouyu,” “Cutting Sandalwood,” and “King Wen”—each preserving archaic lyrics and melody.

sentences.zh: 及太和中，左延年改夔《騶虞》、《伐檀》、《文王》三曲，更自作聲節，其名雖存，而聲實異。

translations.literal: By mid-Taihe, Zuo Yannian revised three of Du Kui’s pieces—“Zouyu,” “Cutting Sandalwood,” and “King Wen”—making fresh rhythmic schemes himself; though titles survived, the actual sound changed.
translations.idiomatic: Mid-Taihe saw Zuo Yannian rework Du Kui’s settings for “Zouyu,” “Cutting Sandalwood,” and “King Wen,” drafting new beats under old names so hearing no longer matched tradition.

translations.literal: Only because of Du Kui’s “Deer Call” did they leave it wholly unchanged.
translations.idiomatic: Only “Deer Call” stayed exactly as Du Kui left it.

sentences.zh: 每正旦大會，太尉奉璧，群後行禮，東廂雅樂常作者是也。

translations.literal: Hence at each New Year’s court assembly, when the Grand Commandant presents the jade disk and regional lords perform ritual, the ritual music regularly performed from the eastern wing is this repertoire.
translations.idiomatic: Thus at dawn court each New Year, when the commander-in-chief lifts the jade tally and kings of domains bow through ceremony, the classical ensemble housed east of the hall repeats these pieces.

translations.literal: Later they again altered the three procession hymns used during ritual.
translations.idiomatic: Later editors swapped the three ceremonial procession poems once more.

sentences.zh: 第一日《於赫篇》，詠武帝，聲節與古《鹿鳴》同。

translations.literal: The first they titled “How Radiant”—praising Emperor Wu—its rhythm matched the ancient “Deer Call.”
translations.idiomatic: Piece one, “How Radiant,” hymned Emperor Wu to the old meter of “Deer Call.”

sentences.zh: 第二曰《巍巍篇》，詠文帝，用延年所改《騶虞》聲。

translations.literal: The second they titled “How Towering”—praising Emperor Wen—using the sound Zuo Yannian had refashioned for “Zouyu.”
translations.idiomatic: Piece two, “How Towering,” praised Emperor Wen with Zuo Yannian’s revised “Zouyu” tune.

sentences.zh: 第三日《洋洋篇》，詠明帝，用延年所改《文王》聲。

translations.literal: The third they titled “How Vast”—praising Emperor Ming—using the sound Zuo Yannian had refashioned for “King Wen.”
translations.idiomatic: Piece three, “How Vast,” honored Emperor Ming with Zuo Yannian’s altered “King Wen” accompaniment.

translations.literal: The fourth returned to employing “Deer Call.”
translations.idiomatic: The fourth slot reused “Deer Call” outright.

translations.literal: Because “Deer Call” was employed twice, they dropped the ancient “Cutting Sandalwood.”
translations.idiomatic: Doubling “Deer Call” pushed out archaic “Cutting Sandalwood.”

translations.literal: When Jin began, banquets at imperial meals likewise used “Deer Call.”
translations.idiomatic: Early Jin court dinners still opened with “Deer Call.”

sentences.zh: 至泰始五年，尚書奏，使太僕傅玄、中書監荀勖、黃門侍郎張華各造正旦行禮及王公上壽酒、食舉樂歌詩。

translations.literal: By the fifth year of Taishi the Secretariat memorialized, ordering Minister Coachman Fu Xuan, Palace Secretariat Director Xun Xu, and Imperial Gate Gentleman Zhang Hua each to compose hymn texts for New Year ritual procession, for princes’ longevity toasts, and for meal-accompaniment music.
translations.idiomatic: Taishi 5 brought a memorial commissioning Fu Xuan, Xun Xu, and Zhang Hua to draft lyrics for New Year ceremonies, royal longevity cups, and feast fanfares.

sentences.zh: 荀勖云：'魏氏行禮、食舉，再取周詩《鹿鳴》以為樂章。

translations.literal: Xun Xu stated: “Wei court ritual and meal music twice borrowed Zhou’s ‘Deer Call’ as its lyrics.
translations.idiomatic: Xun Xu argued, “Wei ceremonies and meal ensembles twice lifted Zhou’s ‘Deer Call’ wholesale.

sentences.zh: 又《鹿鳴》以宴嘉賓，無取於朝，考之舊聞，未知所應。

translations.literal: Moreover ‘Deer Call’ feasts honored guests—it offers nothing suited to court audiences; reviewing ancient precedent, I cannot see how it fits.”
translations.idiomatic: Yet ‘Deer Call’ belongs at banquets for noble visitors, not levee halls; antiquity gives no warrant for recycling it here.”

sentences.zh: 」勖乃除《鹿鳴》舊歌更作行禮詩四篇，先陳三朝朝宗之義。

translations.literal: ” Xu therefore discarded the old “Deer Call” lyrics and wrote four new procession poems opening with the meaning of three-dawn court homage.
translations.idiomatic: So Xun Xu scrapped legacy “Deer Call” text and forged four procession songs foregrounding thrice-yearly court pilgrimage.

sentences.zh: 又為正旦大會、王公上壽歌詩並食舉樂歌詩，合十三篇。

translations.literal: He further composed hymn texts for the great New Year assembly, princes’ longevity toasts, and meal music—thirteen pieces in all.
translations.idiomatic: He added lyrics for the dawn levee, royal toast stanzas, and dining suites—thirteen compositions altogether.

sentences.zh: 又以魏氏歌詩或二言，或三言，或四言，或五言，與古詩不類，以問司律中郎將陳頎。

translations.literal: Moreover because Wei dynasty lyrics sometimes used two, three, four, or five characters per line—unlike ancient poems—he consulted Colonel Director of Pitch Chen Yi.
translations.idiomatic: Because Wei lyrics varied between two and five syllables unlike classical verse, he queried Pitch Colonel Chen Yi.

sentences.zh: 頎曰：「被之金石，未必皆當。

translations.literal: Yi replied: “Once married to bronze and stone, not every line necessarily fits.”
translations.idiomatic: Chen Yi answered, “Fit them to bells and lithophones—not every clause sits equally well.”

sentences.zh: 」故勖造晉歌，皆為四言，唯王公上壽酒一篇為三言五言焉。

translations.literal: ” Hence Xun Xu’s Jin hymns use four-character lines throughout, except one longevity toast mixing three- and five-character verses.
translations.idiomatic: Thus Xun Xu’s Jin corpus stays strictly four-beat lines save the longevity stanza mingling triple and quintuple phrases.

sentences.zh: 張華以為「魏上壽、食舉詩及漢氏所施用，其文句長短不齊，未皆合古。

translations.literal: Zhang Hua held that “Wei longevity and meal poems plus Han adaptations bear uneven line lengths—not all accord with antiquity.
translations.idiomatic: Zhang Hua countered that “Wei toast and banquet lyrics, like Han precedents, stagger line lengths and violate classical meter.

sentences.zh: 蓋以依詠弦節，本有因循，而識樂知音，足以制聲度曲，法用率非凡近之所能改。

translations.literal: Likely because following string rhythms originally allowed inertia; still, those who grasp music can craft measures and bend tunes—normative usage need not bow to vulgar tinkering.
translations.idiomatic: They stuck with instrumental phrasing by habit; yet masters who hear true pattern may forge regulated lines—standard practice should not yield to shallow edits.

sentences.zh: 二代三京，襲而不變，雖詩章辭異，興廢隨時，至其韻逗留曲折，皆系於舊，有由然也。

translations.literal: Two dynasties and three capitals inherited without overhaul; although hymn wording shifted with rise and fall of reigns, cadence lingered and turns twisted along old grooves—and therein lay reason.”
translations.idiomatic: Han and Wei across Luoyang and Ye copied rather than innovated; lyrics rose and fell with politics, yet rhythmic pacing still hugged inherited grooves—and that stubborn continuity had cause.”

sentences.zh: 是以一皆因就，不敢有所改易。

translations.literal: Therefore each piece kept inherited forms—none ventured rash alteration.
translations.idiomatic: So every number hugged precedent—no editor dared novelty.

translations.literal: ” Thus Zhang Hua and Xun Xu disclosed differing intentions.
translations.idiomatic: Here Zhang Hua and Xun Xu laid bare how their aims diverged.

sentences.zh: 時詔又使中書侍郎成公綏亦作焉。

translations.literal: At the same time an edict also ordered Gentleman of the Palace Secretariat Cheng Gongzhao to compose texts.
translations.idiomatic: The court likewise commissioned Secretariat Vice Director Cheng Gongzhao to supply lyrics.

translations.literal: Now both sets are excerpted and recorded below.
translations.idiomatic: What follows preserves both corpora together.

translations.idiomatic: Hymns for the Four Side Galleries

translations.literal: Processional Song for the Great New Year Assembly—by Cheng Gongzhao
translations.idiomatic: Grand Dawn Levee Processional—Cheng Gongzhao

translations.literal: Solemn stands Son of Heaven—his brilliance oversees myriad states.
translations.idiomatic: Grave and luminous the sky son—his radiance spans every kingdom.

translations.literal: Officers crowd the court—none lacks heroic virtue.
translations.idiomatic: Talent packs the hall—not one lacks shining merit.

translations.literal: His transforming influence knows no limit—royal plans truly fill the realm.
translations.idiomatic: Moral sway knows no horizon—imperial strategy saturates the land.

translations.literal: Fine gathering spreads wine—honored guests pack the courtyard.
translations.idiomatic: Blessed convocation raises cups—noble visitors crowd the forecourt.

sentences.zh: 羽旄曜宸極，鐘鼓振泰清。

translations.literal: Feather banners blaze toward polar throne—bells and drums shake Grand Clarity.
translations.idiomatic: Plumed standards glare at zenith seat—bronze storms shake empyrean peace.

sentences.zh: 百辟朝三朝，彧彧明儀形。

translations.literal: Hundred lords attend three audiences—radiant, their ritual bearing.
translations.idiomatic: Regional kings thrice bow at dawn—each pose gleams ordained grace.

translations.literal: Dense ranks clash softly—metal tone jade echo rises.
translations.idiomatic: Crowded rows shimmer—bronze voice answers lithophone shimmer.

translations.literal: Ritual and music stand complete—they feast honored guests.
translations.idiomatic: Ceremony and song assembled—they banquet distinguished callers.

sentences.zh: 眉壽祚聖皇，景福惟日新。

translations.literal: Brow-longevity blesses sage emperor—bright fortune renews daily.
translations.idiomatic: Hoary brows hymn holy sovereign—auspicious blessing refreshes each dawn.

translations.literal: Regional lords arrive together—many come in harmonious throng.
translations.idiomatic: Feudatory kings gather—hosts glide in ordered tide.

translations.literal: They present toasts and submit gifts—they exalt this ritual demeanor.
translations.idiomatic: Gifts pass hand to cup—they magnify this courteous spectacle.

translations.literal: Rich fare fills myriad trenchers—sweet ale stacks thousand goblets.
translations.idiomatic: Savory trays crowd lacquer boards—clear spirits tower in thousand horns.

sentences.zh: 嘉樂盡宴樂，福祿咸攸同。

translations.literal: Glad music exhausts banquet joy—fortune and salary share alike.
translations.idiomatic: Festive air drains the feast—luck and stipend visit everyone.

translations.literal: How joyous!
translations.idiomatic: O what delight!

translations.literal: All under Heaven rests tranquil.
translations.idiomatic: The realm lies undisturbed.

translations.literal: The Way transforms and moves—custom and breeze turn pure.
translations.idiomatic: Virtue rolls outward—folkways clarify like wind-scoured sky.

translations.literal: Panpipes voice Shao music—they chant ninefold perfection.
translations.idiomatic: Flutes raise Shao tunes—they hymn the nine completed strains.

translations.literal: Years heap abundance—the age rests grandly calm.
translations.idiomatic: Harvests pile high—the era sits in ample peace.

translations.literal: Perfect rule indeed—joy knows no end.
translations.idiomatic: Utmost governance—pleasure without boundary.

translations.literal: The sovereign mind acute—thigh and arm prove loyal.
translations.idiomatic: The ruler listens keen—ministers brace him faithful as limbs.

translations.literal: Sweet rains soak—clear breeze lifts.
translations.idiomatic: Timely showers drench—fresh gales fan the realm.

translations.literal: Fine omens emerge—spirit responses blaze.
translations.idiomatic: Bright portents surface—numinous answers flare.

translations.literal: Qilin appears—phoenix soars.
translations.idiomatic: The unicorn steps forth—the fenghuang wheels skyward.

translations.literal: Sweet springs bubble—flow mid courtyard.
translations.idiomatic: Nectar fountains surge—they braid the central yard.

translations.literal: Fine grain sprouts—ears fill bins.
translations.idiomatic: Choice stalks thrive—sheaves cram granary chests.

translations.literal: Dense blessings descend—they bless sage emperor.
translations.idiomatic: Rich grace rains down—it crowns the holy king.

translations.literal: Receiving Heaven’s seat—ruling myriad states.
translations.idiomatic: He takes celestial throne—threads every kingdom on one cord.

sentences.zh: 受命應期，授聖德，四世重光。

translations.literal: Receiving mandate matching its season—handed sacred virtue—four reigns doubled radiance.
translations.idiomatic: Mandate answered its hour—sacred power passed—four reigns stacked glory anew.

sentences.zh: 宣開洪業，景克昌，文欽明，德彌彰。

translations.literal: Xuan opened flooding enterprise—Jing could flourish—Wen revered brilliance—virtue spread wider.
translations.idiomatic: Xuan unfurled vast work—Jing fulfilled expansion—Wen shone discerning—merit widened further.

translations.literal: Thus Jin domain opened—blessings flow without limit.
translations.idiomatic: Thus rose Jin house—fortune streams past horizon.

translations.literal: Taishi founded primal era—phoenix and dragon soar.
translations.idiomatic: Taishi christened first reign—fenghuang and dragon ascend together.

translations.literal: Dragon soaring—how? Enjoying mandate over myriad chariots.
translations.idiomatic: Why dragons climb—to wield fortune across ten thousand cars.

translations.literal: They embrace eight wilds—transform and nurture black-haired folk.
translations.idiomatic: They clasp eight extremities—teaching every common household.

translations.literal: Charts and writings already blaze—metal and stone bear witness.
translations.idiomatic: Oracle graphs flare bright—bells and stones proclaim omen.

translations.literal: Virtue radiates vast—Way glorious and grand.
translations.idiomatic: Merit floods outward—the Path shines towering.

translations.literal: Covering beyond four frontiers—it penetrates royal dome.
translations.idiomatic: It mantles four shores—it pierces celestial vault.

sentences.zh: 奕奕萬嗣，明明顯融，高朗令終。

translations.literal: Flourishing heirs beyond count—brilliant merge on high—noble clarity meets fitting close.
translations.idiomatic: Successors teem radiant—glories fuse aloft—bright ends crown noble reigns.

translations.literal: Guard this eternal throne—rival Heaven’s height.
translations.idiomatic: Hold this endless mandate—match august Heaven’s stature.

sentences.zh: 聖皇君四海，順人應天期。

translations.literal: Sage emperor rules four seas—following men he answers Heaven’s season.
translations.idiomatic: Holy king masters four oceans—yielding to people he meets celestial clock.

sentences.zh: 三葉合重光，泰始開洪基。

translations.literal: Three generations stack doubled radiance—Taishi opens flooding foundation.
translations.idiomatic: Three reigns layer doubled gleam—Taishi splits primordial cornerstone.

sentences.zh: 明曜參日月，功化侔四時。

translations.literal: Bright glory pairs sun and moon—merit rivals four seasons.
